items.claim: Anonymous LDAP bind on a domain controller can expose user accounts, groups, and directory structure without credentials.
items.body: Some LDAP servers allow anonymous read queries. Test with ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC -s base. If successful, enumerate users with (objectClass=person) and groups with (objectClass=group). Anonymous bind is a common misconfiguration that leaks the entire directory.
items.disproof: Anonymous bind is disabled and returns insufficientAccessRights.

sources.quote: Some LDAP servers allow anonymous users to perform read-only queries.
Anonymous Bind: Try connecting without credentials.

items.claim: LDAP injection occurs when user input is concatenated into an LDAP filter, allowing an attacker to alter query logic and bypass authentication.
items.body: Applications building LDAP filters from user input (e.g., (&(uid=INPUT)(password=INPUT))) are vulnerable. Injecting * or )(uid=*))(& can bypass filters. Special characters like *, (, ), |, & manipulate filter logic similarly to SQL injection but against directory queries.
items.disproof: Input is escaped per RFC 4515 or parameterized queries are used.

sources.quote: LDAP injection exploits applications that construct LDAP queries from user-supplied input.
LDAP is a goldmine for enumeration.

items.claim: Nmap LDAP scripts enumerate naming contexts, users, and groups from a domain controller on ports 389 and 636.
items.body: Run nmap -n -sV --script 'ldap* and not brute' -p 389 DC_IP to extract LDAP root DSE and naming contexts. Follow up with ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC -b 'DC=domain,DC=local' '(objectclass=*)' to dump the directory. Authenticated binds provide full user and group enumeration.
items.disproof: LDAP ports are filtered or the server requires signing and rejects the query.
